title: Week 4 · Lesson 12: Heart Failure — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 4 — Lesson 12: Heart Failure

FNP-level goal

Use hemodynamics to distinguish systolic from diastolic dysfunction, connect congestion to renal and pulmonary physiology, interpret BNP/NT-proBNP in context, and recognize when dyspnea or edema requires emergency escalation rather than routine outpatient management.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate HFrEF from HFpEF using contraction, relaxation, chamber structure, and filling pressures.
  • Explain forward hypoperfusion and backward congestion.
  • Connect SNS/RAAS compensation to fluid retention, remodeling, and worsening heart failure.
  • Explain pulmonary edema, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and right-sided systemic congestion.
  • Build a focused differential and initial diagnostic/disposition plan for dyspnea and edema.

Part 1 — What heart failure means

Heart failure is a clinical syndrome in which the heart cannot meet the body’s metabolic needs without abnormal filling pressures and/or compensatory activation. It is not simply “a weak heart.” A patient may have reduced forward flow, elevated filling pressures, venous congestion, or several of these at once.

Two high-yield patterns are HFrEF, where systolic contraction is impaired, and HFpEF, where ejection fraction is preserved but the ventricle is stiff and fills at abnormally high pressure. A preserved EF does not mean normal cardiac function.

Part 2 — Ejection fraction and HFrEF

Ejection fraction is the proportion of end-diastolic ventricular volume ejected with systole: EF = stroke volume / end-diastolic volume × 100%. In HFrEF, myocardial injury or dysfunction reduces contractility, lowering stroke volume, cardiac output, and EF. Prior MI, ischemic cardiomyopathy, dilated cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, toxins, and some valve disorders can contribute.

After an MI, necrotic myocardium cannot contract. Loss of functional muscle plus adverse remodeling can dilate the ventricle, raise wall stress, and produce progressive systolic dysfunction.

Part 3 — HFpEF: a filling-pressure problem

In HFpEF, contraction may appear relatively preserved, but impaired relaxation and ventricular stiffness mean the ventricle fills poorly. A higher filling pressure is required to achieve adequate filling; that pressure is transmitted backward to the left atrium and pulmonary veins.

Chronic hypertension is a classic pathway: afterload increases → LV hypertrophy develops → the ventricle stiffens → diastolic filling is impaired → left-sided filling pressures rise. Aging, obesity, diabetes, CKD, atrial fibrillation, and valvular disease frequently coexist and can worsen this phenotype.

Part 4 — Forward failure and backward congestion

Forward failure refers to inadequate effective cardiac output. Patients can experience fatigue, weakness, exercise intolerance, cool extremities, renal hypoperfusion, and—when severe—altered mentation or shock.

Backward congestion occurs when pressure rises behind the failing chamber. Elevated left-sided filling pressure raises pulmonary venous and capillary hydrostatic pressure; elevated right-sided pressure raises systemic venous pressure. These are hemodynamic consequences, not separate diseases.

Part 5 — Pulmonary edema and dyspnea

LV dysfunction or high LV filling pressure → left atrial pressure ↑ → pulmonary venous pressure ↑ → pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure ↑ → fluid moves into the lung interstitium and alveoli. Fluid increases diffusion distance, creates low V/Q regions, decreases compliance, and raises the work of breathing. The result can be dyspnea, crackles, hypoxemia, and exercise intolerance.

Orthopnea is dyspnea when supine. Venous return and fluid redistribution increase preload, which a failing or stiff LV may not tolerate. Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea is sudden nighttime dyspnea related to worsening congestion while supine.

Part 6 — Right-sided congestion

Right ventricular failure raises right atrial and systemic venous pressure, producing dependent edema, elevated jugular venous pressure, hepatic congestion, and ascites. Left-sided heart failure can eventually increase pulmonary vascular pressure and RV afterload, so left and right failure often coexist.

Edema alone does not diagnose heart failure. Kidney disease, venous disease, liver disease, medications, low oncotic pressure, and lymphatic disease belong in the differential. Determine whether the hemodynamics and overall presentation support congestion from HF.

Part 7 — Compensation becomes maladaptive

When effective cardiac output falls, baroreceptor and renal signals activate the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) and RAAS. SNS increases heart rate, contractility, and vascular tone. RAAS increases angiotensin II-mediated vasoconstriction and aldosterone-mediated sodium/water retention. Initially, this can help maintain perfusion.

Chronically, the same response increases afterload, preload, oxygen demand, arrhythmia risk, congestion, fibrosis, and remodeling. The critical cycle is: cardiac dysfunction → SNS/RAAS → vasoconstriction and volume retention → higher workload/filling pressure → worsening dysfunction.

Part 8 — BNP and NT-proBNP: useful, not standalone

Ventricular wall stretch and increased filling pressure promote release of natriuretic peptides. BNP promotes natriuresis, diuresis, and vasodilation—effects that oppose RAAS. BNP or NT-proBNP can support or help exclude heart failure when the clinical diagnosis is uncertain, especially in a patient with dyspnea.

Do not let one value replace clinical reasoning. Kidney function, age, obesity, atrial arrhythmias, and other cardiac conditions can affect levels. Diagnosis integrates history, vital signs, examination, ECG, imaging, laboratory data, and echocardiography when indicated.

Part 9 — Why diuresis and disease-modifying therapy are different

When congestion is present, increasing renal sodium and water excretion can lower filling pressure and improve dyspnea and edema. This explains the symptomatic role of diuresis. Long-term outcome improvement in eligible patients, especially in HFrEF, also depends on addressing maladaptive neurohormonal pathways and the underlying cause. Therapy selection and titration must be individualized to blood pressure, renal function, potassium, rhythm, comorbidities, and volume status.

Part 10 — Acute decompensation: recognize danger early

Severe respiratory distress, hypoxemia, pulmonary edema, hypotension, chest pain concerning for ACS, syncope, altered mental status, cool/clammy extremities, or rapidly declining urine output indicate possible acute decompensated HF, cardiogenic shock, or another emergency. Do not continue an outpatient workup in an unstable patient.

Possible precipitants include ACS/MI, arrhythmia, severe hypertension, infection, medication or dietary factors, kidney dysfunction, anemia, valvular disease, pulmonary embolism, and nonadherence. The FNP task is to recognize instability, initiate appropriate emergency transfer, and communicate the clinical pattern and potential trigger.

Case 1 — Preserved EF, real heart failure

A 72-year-old with longstanding hypertension has exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, edema, and EF 60%. Do not dismiss HF because EF is “normal.” Chronic afterload can create LV hypertrophy and stiffness; elevated filling pressure can produce pulmonary congestion. HFpEF is a clinical possibility requiring integrated evaluation.

Case 2 — MI followed by congestion

A 65-year-old with prior MI, EF 30%, fatigue, orthopnea, and leg edema has HFrEF physiology: loss of contractile myocardium → lower stroke volume/EF → SNS and RAAS activation → volume retention and congestion. Renal function and potassium matter because heart and kidney physiology are inseparable here.

Case 3 — Dyspnea with an elevated BNP

A patient has dyspnea, edema, and elevated BNP. BNP supports a heart-failure hypothesis but does not make the diagnosis alone. Assess symptoms, vital signs, examination, ECG, chest imaging when appropriate, renal function, rhythm, prior cardiac disease, and alternative causes such as pulmonary disease, PE, anemia, or kidney disease.

FNP High-Yield Framework

  1. Is the patient stable? Check oxygenation, work of breathing, perfusion, mental status, chest pain, and blood pressure.
  2. Is there congestion, low output, or both?
  3. Consider HFrEF versus HFpEF, but do not use EF alone to rule out HF.
  4. Look for triggers: ischemia, arrhythmia, severe hypertension, infection, renal dysfunction, valve disease, or medication factors.
  5. Use BNP/NT-proBNP and testing as supportive evidence, not a single-test diagnosis.
  6. Choose disposition early: stable outpatient evaluation, expedited cardiovascular review, or emergency care.

High-Yield Summary

HFrEF: impaired contraction → EF reduced.
HFpEF: impaired relaxation/stiff ventricle → elevated filling pressure despite preserved EF.
Left HF: pulmonary venous congestion → dyspnea, orthopnea, pulmonary edema.
Right HF: systemic venous congestion → edema, JVD, hepatic congestion, ascites.
SNS/RAAS: initially support perfusion but chronically increase afterload, volume, and remodeling.
BNP: marker of wall stretch/filling pressure; interpret with clinical context.
Emergency red flags: severe dyspnea/hypoxemia, pulmonary edema, shock, syncope, ongoing concerning chest pain, or altered mentation.
